trig-inverse-functions-inverse-sine-cosi.title: Inverse sine, cosine, and tangent
trig-inverse-functions-inverse-sine-cosi.summary: Define arcsin, arccos and arctan as principal-value inverses, not reciprocals; evaluate exact inputs using restricted ranges.

blocks.text: The inverses of sine, cosine and tangent return one principal angle. The input of an inverse function is a trigonometric ratio, and the output is an angle. Arcsin, arccos and arctan are NOT 1/sin, 1/cos or 1/tan.

blocks.title: Find arcsin(−1/2)
blocks.strategy: Use the sine principal range from −90° to +90°.
blocks.check: sin(−π/6)=−1/2; the chosen angle is in the principal range.

blocks.title: Find arccos(−1/2)
blocks.strategy: Choose an angle in the cosine principal range 0 to π.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint and reference guide

blocks.text: Do not interchange arcsin and cosecant. A calculator in degree mode displays degree-valued angles, but the exact answers in these lessons use radians unless otherwise specified.

Reference guide: Lial, Trigonometry, 10th ed., §6.1 (pp. 246–261); Young, Trigonometry, 3rd ed., §6.1; Sullivan, Trigonometry, 9th ed., §§3.1–3.2; Schaum’s Outline, 4th ed., Ch. 13; Kelley, Humongous Book, Ch. 9. Verify printed versus PDF pagination before using page references in lesson text.

trig-inverse-functions-inverse-secant-co.title: Inverse secant, cosecant, and cotangent conventions
trig-inverse-functions-inverse-secant-co.summary: Use an explicit branch convention for arcsec, arccsc and arccot; explain why other references may choose different branches.

blocks.text: Inverse secant, cosecant and cotangent require specified principal branches. In this app, arcsec(x)=arccos(1/x) for |x|≥1; arccsc(x)=arcsin(1/x) for |x|≥1; arccot(x) takes values strictly between 0 and π, with cot(arccot x)=x. Some references use a different arccot branch; always check the convention.

blocks.title: Evaluate arcsec(−2)
blocks.strategy: Convert to arccos of the reciprocal.
steps: The angle 2π/3 has cosine −1/2 and lies in the required range.

blocks.title: Evaluate arccot(−1)
blocks.strategy: Select an angle in (0,π), not the arctangent principal range.
blocks.check: cot(3π/4)=−1; 3π/4 is inside the declared branch.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint and reference guide

blocks.text: The expression arccot(−1) has convention-dependent answers. For this lesson it equals 3π/4, not −π/4; disclose the chosen range in each question.

blocks.prompt: Under the declared convention, what is arccsc(−2)?

trig-inverse-functions-principal-values-.title: Principal values and domain restrictions
trig-inverse-functions-principal-values-.summary: Determine valid inputs and output branches, and distinguish principal solutions from all angles sharing the same trigonometric value.

blocks.text: An inverse trigonometric function is defined by restricting a periodic function to a one-to-one branch. For arcsin and arccos, inputs outside [−1,1] have no real output. The inverse-function output is one principal angle; the general solution of sinθ=a may have infinitely many angles.

blocks.title: Find the real domain of arcsin(2x−1)
blocks.problem: Find the real domain of arcsin(2x−1)
blocks.strategy: The arcsin input must lie between −1 and 1.
blocks.check: Both endpoints are included: arcsin(−1) and arcsin(1) are real.

blocks.title: Evaluate arcsin(sin(5π/6))
blocks.strategy: First evaluate sine, then return its principal angle.
blocks.check: π/6 is in [−π/2,π/2] and has sine 1/2.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint and reference guide

blocks.text: Do not cancel arcsin(sinθ) unless θ is on the chosen branch; solving sinθ=a is different from evaluating arcsin(a).

blocks.prompt: Does arccos(1.2) have a real value?
blocks.explanation: The real domain of arccos is [−1,1], and 1.2 lies outside it.

trig-inverse-functions-graphs-of-inverse.title: Graphs of inverse trig functions
trig-inverse-functions-graphs-of-inverse.summary: Interpret inverse graphs as reflections across y=x of the restricted original functions, including endpoints and asymptotes.

blocks.text: The inverse function graph swaps x and y after the original trigonometric function is restricted to a one-to-one branch. Arcsin is increasing from (−1,−π/2) to (1,π/2); arccos is decreasing from (−1,π) to (1,0); arctan increases with horizontal asymptotes y=±π/2.

blocks.caption: Arcsin (teal), arccos (purple), and arctan (orange) shown on their principal branches; closed endpoints for arcsin/arccos and horizontal asymptotes for arctan.

blocks.title: Find the y-intercept of y=arccos x
blocks.problem: Find the y-intercept of y=arccos x
blocks.check: cos(π/2)=0 and π/2 is on the arccos principal branch.

blocks.title: Identify the upper asymptote of y=arctan x
blocks.problem: Identify the upper asymptote of y=arctan x
steps: The arctangent output remains strictly between −π/2 and π/2.
As x→+∞, arctan x approaches π/2 from below.
blocks.check: The horizontal asymptote y=π/2 is not part of the range.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint and reference guide

blocks.text: Arcsin and arccos do not have horizontal asymptotes at their endpoints: both have closed endpoints. Arctan has asymptotes but never reaches ±π/2.

blocks.prompt: Is y=arccos x increasing or decreasing?
blocks.explanation: On [−1,1], larger x requires a smaller angle in [0,π] to have that cosine value.

trig-inverse-functions-exact-inverse-fun.title: Exact inverse-function values
trig-inverse-functions-exact-inverse-fun.summary: Compute exact inverse-function values using standard triangles and quadrant restrictions without unnecessary decimal approximations.

blocks.text: Exact answers are principal angles often expressed as rational multiples of π. Identify the trigonometric ratio, locate all standard-angle candidates, then choose the unique angle in the declared inverse-function range.

blocks.title: Evaluate arccos(−√2/2)
blocks.strategy: Use the reference angle π/4, then choose the cosine-negative candidate in [0,π].
blocks.check: 3π/4 lies in the cosine inverse range, not in arcsin’s range.

blocks.title: Evaluate arcsin(−√3/2)
blocks.strategy: Select a negative angle in the arcsin range.
steps: Since −π/3 is inside [−π/2,π/2], the exact answer is −π/3.
blocks.check: A positive 4π/3 has the same sine but is not the inverse sine principal value.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint and reference guide

blocks.text: Exact input values such as √3/2 are ratios, not angle measures. Always check a candidate against the principal interval before choosing it.

blocks.explanation: tan(π/6)=1/√3 and π/6 belongs to the arctangent principal interval.

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial, Trigonometry, 10th ed., §6.1 (pp. 246–261); Young, Trigonometry, 3rd ed., §6.1; Sullivan, Trigonometry, 9th ed., §§3.1–3.2; Schaum’s Outline, 4th ed., Ch. 13; Kelley, Humongous Book, Ch. 9. trig-inverse-functions-compositions-with.title: Compositions with inverse functions
trig-inverse-functions-compositions-with.summary: Simplify trig–inverse compositions and inverse–trig compositions, preserving input domains, output branches, and positive square-root choices.

blocks.text: For a principal inverse θ=arccos x, θ lies in [0,π] so sinθ≥0. For θ=arcsin x, θ lies in [−π/2,π/2] so cosθ≥0. These sign facts fix the correct square root when simplifying compositions. Inverse–trig compositions such as arcsin(sinθ) are only identity functions within the inverse branch.

blocks.title: Simplify cos(arcsin(3/5))
blocks.strategy: Draw a right triangle with opposite 3, hypotenuse 5, and nonnegative adjacent side.
steps: Let θ=arcsin(3/5); then sinθ=3/5 and θ∈[−π/2,π/2].
blocks.check: Cosine is nonnegative on the entire arcsin principal range.

blocks.title: Evaluate arccos(cos(5π/3))
blocks.strategy: The input angle need not lie in arccos’s principal interval.
steps: arccos(1/2)=π/3; 5π/3 is not the answer because it lies outside [0,π].
blocks.check: cos(π/3)=1/2, and π/3 is the principal cosine angle.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint and reference guide

blocks.text: Do not use ±√(1−x²) for cos(arcsin x): the branch fixes the nonnegative sign. tan(arcsin x) excludes x=±1 because its denominator vanishes.

blocks.explanation: The arccos angle lies in quadrant II where sine is nonnegative, so √(1−16/25)=3/5.
